city.moldStory: Dayton combines one of the oldest housing stocks in the Miami Valley — roughly three-quarters of homes predate 1980, with many downtown and inner neighborhoods built before 1950 — with freeze-thaw winters that drive ice dams and attic moisture, and humid summers that feed basement and crawl-space mold. The Great Miami River floodplain adds periodic water-intrusion events, and the city's aging brick duplexes and rental stock often hide long-term moisture problems behind walls.
city.name: Dayton

climate.avgHumidityNote: Humid continental climate (NOAA 30-year normals). Summer humidity routinely pushes indoor levels above 60% (EPA recommends 30–50% indoors); winter brings freeze-thaw cycles, ice dams, and condensation in closed-up homes.
climate.moldSeasonNote: Peak mold pressure May through September (humidity + thunderstorms); spring flooding along the Great Miami River watershed; winter brings ice-dam attic mold and pipe-burst water damage. Effectively a year-round market.

state.licensingNote: Ohio has no statewide mold assessor or remediator licensing requirement (unlike Florida, Texas, and New York, which do license mold professionals; no Ohio-specific mold license found in current state code — Ohio licenses lead abatement, not mold). Contractors should follow EPA and IICRC S520 remediation guidelines; homeowners should verify any contractor's general credentials and insurance.
state.moldStory: Ohio's humid continental climate — roughly 40 inches of annual rainfall, muggy summers, and freeze-thaw winters — makes mold a statewide, year-round issue. The Miami Valley's older housing stock (much of it pre-1980) plus Great Miami River floodplain moisture create persistent moisture-intrusion risk, from ice-dam attic mold in winter to basement and crawl-space mold in the humid summer months.
state.name: Ohio

towns.moldStory: Kettering's housing stock is among the oldest in the metro (median build year ~1961), with 1950s–60s ranch homes whose aging roofs, original windows, and basements are prime mold territory. Mature tree cover keeps many homes shaded and damp, compounding moisture issues.
towns.name: Kettering

towns.moldStory: Beavercreek skews newer (median build ~1981) but its rapid expansion over former farmland means many homes sit on high water tables; finished basements are common and humid summers drive crawl-space and basement mold calls. Older pockets like Knollwood mix 1950s homes with newer builds.
towns.name: Beavercreek

towns.moldStory: Built largely in the 1960s–70s suburban boom ('Brick City'), Huber Heights has miles of aging brick ranch homes where deteriorating flashing, old gutters, and basement seepage create steady mold-remediation demand.
towns.name: Huber Heights

towns.moldStory: Centerville mixes historic stone homes in Uptown (some on the National Register) with 1970s–90s subdivisions; older stone foundations wick moisture, while mature trees and shaded lots keep humidity high around foundations.
towns.name: Centerville

towns.moldStory: Fairborn's older neighborhoods near Wright-Patterson AFB feature mid-century homes with aging plumbing and flat-roof additions; heavy student-rental turnover near Wright State means deferred maintenance and hidden mold behind walls and under sinks.
towns.name: Fairborn

towns.moldStory: Springboro is the metro's newest suburb (population up ~53% since 2000), so mold risk here is less about age and more about construction — rapid-build subdivisions with grading and drainage issues, plus humid summers stressing crawl spaces in newer homes.
towns.name: Springboro

towns.moldStory: Troy's 19th-century downtown and early-1900s neighborhoods along the Great Miami River combine old plaster-and-lath homes with periodic river flooding — a classic recipe for hidden wall-cavity mold.
towns.name: Troy

towns.moldStory: Piqua's industrial-era housing stock (founded 1807, much of it pre-1970) and low-lying areas near the Great Miami River and its canal-era infrastructure mean chronic basement moisture — the city's most common mold driver.
towns.name: Piqua

towns.moldStory: Much of Xenia was rebuilt after the devastating 1974 tornado destroyed nearly half the city, creating a patchwork of 1970s rebuilds now hitting 50 years old — aging roofs and siding at exactly the age when moisture intrusion, and mold, accelerates.
towns.name: Xenia

towns.moldStory: Sidney's 19th-century downtown core and early-1900s worker housing near the Great Miami River sit in one of the metro's older housing stocks, with stone foundations and aging roofs that trap moisture — compounded by its position ~36 miles north of Dayton in the river valley.
towns.name: Sidney
